subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 24-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation has vaginal bleeding, severe vomiting, and a uterine size larger than expected for dates. She has pelvic pressure and a blood pressure of 150/95 mm Hg. Ultrasound shows a honeycombed uterus with a snowstorm appearance and no identifiable fetus.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hydatidiform mole
Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Placenta previa
Multifetal gestation

explanation_correct: Hydatidiform mole is cystic swelling of chorionic villi with trophoblastic proliferation. It presents with vaginal bleeding, emesis, uterine enlargement greater than expected, and pelvic pressure/pain. Very high hCG produces sequelae including hyperthyroidism, theca lutein cysts, hyperemesis gravidarum, and preeclampsia before 20 weeks. The honeycombed or snowstorm ultrasound with no fetus is classic. Treatment is dilation and curettage with or without methotrexate and hCG monitoring.

explanation_incorrect.B: Placental abruption presents with painful third-trimester bleeding and hypertension but would not produce a snowstorm uterus or a uterus large for dates with no fetus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ectopic pregnancy is a first-trimester adnexal gestation with lower-than-expected hCG, not a enlarged honeycombed uterus with markedly elevated hCG.
explanation_incorrect.D: Placenta previa causes painless vaginal bleeding from placenta over the os but lacks the hCG sequelae and snowstorm appearance described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Multifetal gestation can cause a uterus large for dates but would show fetuses on ultrasound and not the characteristic snowstorm or extreme hCG elevation.

educationalObjective: Hydatidiform mole presents with bleeding, uterus large for dates, hyperemesis, early preeclampsia, and a snowstorm ultrasound from high hCG.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: Products of conception from a molar pregnancy show hydropic villi with circumferential, diffuse trophoblastic proliferation and no fetal parts. Immunostain for p57 is negative. The genetics counselor explains that this is the most common androgenetic diploid mole.
question: Which of the following best describes the karyotype and origin of this mole?

options.text: 69,XXX from fertilization of one egg by two sperm
46,XY from an enucleated egg fertilized by two sperm
46,XX (most common) from an enucleated egg fertilized by a single sperm that duplicates paternal DNA
69,XXY from two sperm fertilizing one egg
46,XX from normal fertilization with equal maternal and paternal DNA

explanation_correct: A complete mole is most commonly 46,XX (and sometimes 46,XY) and arises when an enucleated egg is fertilized by a single sperm that then duplicates its paternal DNA, making the genome entirely paternal. Histology shows hydropic villi with circumferential, diffuse trophoblastic proliferation and no fetal parts; p57 is negative because the gene is maternally expressed. Uterine size and hCG are markedly increased, with a honeycombed/snowstorm ultrasound. This is the 'complete male' mole.

explanation_incorrect.A: A 69,XXX karyotype from two sperm plus one egg is a partial mole, not a complete mole, and would have fetal parts and focal proliferation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Two sperm fertilizing an enucleated egg would not produce the typical 46,XX complete mole; a single sperm duplicating its DNA is the mechanism.
explanation_incorrect.D: A 69,XXY karyotype from two sperm plus one egg is a partial mole, which is triploid and p57 positive.
explanation_incorrect.E: Normal fertilization with maternal and paternal DNA yields a normal conceptus, not an androgenetic complete mole with p57 negativity.

educationalObjective: Complete mole is 46,XX (or 46,XY) from an enucleated egg plus a duplicated single sperm: diffuse trophoblast, no fetus, p57 negative, very high hCG.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has a molar pregnancy. Examination of the products of conception shows only some hydropic villi with focal, minimal trophoblastic proliferation, and fetal parts are present. Her hCG is only modestly elevated and p57 immunostain is positive.
question: Which of the following set of findings best characterizes this partial mole?

options.text: 46,XX; no fetal parts; p57 negative; markedly elevated hCG
Diffuse circumferential trophoblastic proliferation with a snowstorm ultrasound
Enucleated egg fertilized by a single sperm that duplicates its DNA
Uterine size much larger than expected with hCG elevated fourfold
69,XXX/XXY/XYY from two sperm plus one egg, with focal trophoblastic proliferation, fetal parts, and p57 positivity

explanation_correct: A partial mole is triploid, most often 69,XXX, 69,XXY, or 69,XYY, resulting from fertilization of one egg by two sperm. Only some villi are hydropic, trophoblastic proliferation is focal or minimal, and fetal parts are present. p57 is positive because maternally expressed DNA is retained, and hCG is only moderately elevated. It carries a low risk of invasive mole and rarely progresses to choriocarcinoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: A 46,XX androgenetic mole with no fetal parts, p57 negativity, and very high hCG describes a complete mole, not a partial mole.
explanation_incorrect.B: Diffuse circumferential trophoblastic proliferation with a snowstorm appearance is characteristic of a complete mole.
explanation_incorrect.C: An enucleated egg fertilized by a single sperm that duplicates its DNA is the mechanism of a complete mole.
explanation_incorrect.D: A uterus much larger than expected with markedly elevated hCG is typical of a complete mole, not a partial mole.

educationalObjective: Partial mole is triploid (69,XXX/XXY/XYY) with two sperm plus one egg, focal trophoblastic proliferation, fetal parts, p57 positive, and modest hCG.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A pathology resident is reviewing p57 immunohistochemical staining to distinguish complete from partial moles. She recalls that p57 is a maternally expressed, paternally imprinted gene product and that the presence or absence of maternal DNA determines the staining pattern.
question: Which of the following statements about p57 staining in molar pregnancy is correct?

options.text: p57 is paternally expressed, so a complete mole is p57 positive
p57 is maternally expressed and paternally imprinted; a complete mole lacks maternal DNA and is p57 negative, whereas a partial mole is p57 positive
p57 is negative in partial mole and positive in complete mole because of paternal imprinting
p57 staining identifies the presence of fetal parts rather than trophoblastic tissue
p57 is equally positive in complete and partial moles and cannot distinguish them

explanation_correct: p57 is maternally expressed and paternally imprinted. A complete mole contains only paternal DNA (enucleated egg plus duplicated sperm DNA), so there is no maternal p57 expression and the specimen is p57 negative — the 'complete male' mole. A partial mole retains maternal DNA from the egg and is p57 positive. This immunostain is a key tool for distinguishing the two entities.

explanation_incorrect.A: p57 is maternally expressed, not paternally expressed, and a complete mole is p57 negative because it lacks maternal DNA.
explanation_incorrect.C: The pattern is reversed: complete mole is p57 negative and partial mole is p57 positive.
explanation_incorrect.D: p57 is an immunostain for a maternally expressed gene product, not a marker that simply identifies fetal parts.
explanation_incorrect.E: p57 staining reliably differs between complete (negative) and partial (positive) moles and is useful in the differential diagnosis.

educationalObjective: p57 is maternally expressed/paternally imprinted: complete mole (no maternal DNA) is p57 negative; partial mole is p57 positive.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 26-year-old woman is diagnosed with a complete hydatidiform mole and treated with dilation and curettage. Before discharge, she asks about her risk of developing an invasive mole or choriocarcinoma and what follow-up she will need. The counselor reviews the malignant potential of complete versus partial moles.
question: Which of the following best states the malignant potential and management of a complete mole?

options.text: A complete mole has a <5% risk of invasive mole and rarely progresses to choriocarcinoma
No further hCG monitoring is required once the mole has been curetted
A complete mole carries a 2% risk of invasive mole and a 15–20% risk of choriocarcinoma
A complete mole has a 15–20% risk of invasive mole and about a 2% risk of choriocarcinoma; treat with dilation and curettage with or without methotrexate and monitor hCG
Hysterectomy is required for every complete mole regardless of childbearing plans

explanation_correct: A complete mole has approximately a 15–20% risk of invasive mole and about a 2% risk of progressing to choriocarcinoma, whereas a partial mole has a <5% risk of invasive mole and only rare choriocarcinoma. Treatment is dilation and curettage with or without methotrexate, followed by serial hCG monitoring to detect persistent or malignant trophoblastic disease. Hysterectomy is not routinely required.

explanation_incorrect.A: A <5% risk of invasive mole and rare choriocarcinoma describes a partial mole, not a complete mole.
explanation_incorrect.B: Serial hCG monitoring after curettage is essential to detect persistent trophoblastic disease or malignant transformation.
explanation_incorrect.C: The percentages are reversed: invasive mole risk is 15–20% and choriocarcinoma risk is about 2% for a complete mole.
explanation_incorrect.E: Dilation and curettage, not routine hysterectomy, is the standard treatment; hysterectomy is reserved for specific circumstances.

educationalObjective: Complete mole: 15–20% invasive mole, ~2% choriocarcinoma; manage with D&C ± methotrexate and serial hCG monitoring.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 27-year-old woman had a hydatidiform mole 3 months ago. She now has abnormal uterine bleeding, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Chest imaging shows multiple rounded 'cannonball' metastases, and her serum hCG is markedly elevated.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Choriocarcinoma
Invasive mole confined to the uterus
Placental abruption
Ectopic pregnancy
Pulmonary embolism from a deep vein thrombosis

explanation_correct: Choriocarcinoma is a rare malignancy of trophoblastic tissue (cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts) without chorionic villi. It most often follows an abnormal pregnancy such as a hydatidiform mole or abortion and can arise nongestationally in the gonads. It presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, hCG-mediated sequelae, dyspnea, and hemoptysis from hematogenous lung metastases described as cannonball lesions. Treatment is methotrexate.

explanation_incorrect.B: An invasive mole retains chorionic villi and does not typically produce the widely disseminated cannonball lung metastases described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Placental abruption is an acute third-trimester event with painful bleeding, not a distant metastatic process after a mole.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ectopic pregnancy would not follow a molar pregnancy months later with lung metastases and markedly elevated hCG.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pulmonary embolism can cause dyspnea but would not explain the abnormal uterine bleeding, elevated hCG, or cannonball metastases.

educationalObjective: Choriocarcinoma follows abnormal pregnancy, has no chorionic villi, spreads hematogenously to lungs as cannonball metastases, and is treated with methotrexate.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 30-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and a hemorrhagic, necrotic uterine mass several months after a spontaneous abortion. Histology shows a dimorphic population of malignant cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts. No chorionic villi are identified. She has elevated hCG and lung nodules.
question: Which histologic feature best distinguishes this lesion from a hydatidiform mole?

options.text: Hydropic chorionic villi with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation
Focal trophoblastic proliferation with fetal parts and only modest hCG elevation
Umbilical cord vessels protected by Wharton jelly
Chorionic villi with molar swelling and a snowstorm ultrasound appearance
Malignant cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts without any chorionic villi

explanation_correct: Choriocarcinoma is a malignant proliferation of trophoblastic tissue (cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts) that is defined by the absence of chorionic villi. It typically arises after an abnormal pregnancy such as a mole or abortion, or nongestationally in the gonads, and presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, hCG sequelae, and hematogenous cannonball lung metastases. Hydatidiform moles, by contrast, always contain chorionic villi that are hydropically swollen. Treatment is methotrexate.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hydropic villi with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation is the histology of a complete mole, which retains villi.
explanation_incorrect.B: Focal trophoblastic proliferation with fetal parts and modest hCG describes a partial mole, not a villa-less malignancy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Wharton jelly surrounds cord vessels and relates to vasa previa, not to distinguishing choriocarcinoma from mole.
explanation_incorrect.D: Molar chorionic villi with a snowstorm ultrasound indicate a hydatidiform mole, whereas choriocarcinoma has no villi.

educationalObjective: Choriocarcinoma lacks chorionic villi and shows malignant cytotrophoblast/syncytiotrophoblast; moles retain hydropic villi.
